name: Kabwari
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Although there is no information extant for the Bwari language, it is probable that it corresponds to so-called "kabwari" (J-56) of Guthrie (1967). My research showed that it has 5 vowels like other J-languages. All these are tone languages having principally a high tone and a low tone. Table 2 summarizes the linguistic traits of Songola and Bwari languages. [...] [Table 2A, Bwari (J.56)] tones: High: /´/. Low: without tone marks, except for consonants having one mora such as /m̂/ and /n̂/.
new_statements.citation: Ankei, Yuji. 1989. Folk Knowledge of Fish among the Songola and the Bwari: Comparative Ethnoichthyology of the Lualaba River and Lake Tanganyika Fishermen. African Study Monographs, Supplementary Issue 9: 1-88. Kyoto University.
new_statements.locator: p. 5 (sec. on languages) and Table 2A 'Phonemes of Songola-Enya and Bwari', row 'tones' (PDF page 5)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

Low: without tone marks, except for consonants h…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kabwari (Bwari) is described only as a two-tone (H vs L) Bantu language with five vowels; the author marks H with an acute on his Bwari fish-name data. No statement about word stress or accent placement exists in this or any other source located. (French version, Ankei 1986: 6: 'Toutes les langues citées sont tonales; elles ont un ton haut et un ton bas'; Japanese original, Ankei 1982: 4-5, same content.)
new_statements.exceptions: None. The author notes tones were elicited by having informants add a possessive ('my') to each noun to stabilise them (described for Songola; Bwari names are likewise tone-marked).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on isolated nouns (fish names, noun-class prefixes); nothing on phrase-level prosody, vowel-length/penultimate lengthening, or citation-form accent. The author is an ecological anthropologist, not a linguist; 45 days of fieldwork among the Bwari in 1979.
new_statements.identity_note: Ankei's 'Bwari' are the fishing people of the Ubwari peninsula near Baraka (Fizi territory, South Kivu, NW shore of Lake Tanganyika); Ankei himself states it 'probably corresponds to so-called kabwari (J-56) of Guthrie', i.e. Glottolog kabw1242 / ISO kcw (Maho JD56). Same variety as the target; no dialect differentiation reported. Note Bastin 2003 flags that Bwari's affiliation (Zone J vs Zone D/Bembe D54) is not fully settled.
